title: Authentication Flaws
subtitle: Weak passwords, brute force, credential stuffing, and how to implement authentication that actually holds up

content.code:
WEAK PASSWORD POLICIES:
  Allowing 'password123', '123456', common words
  No minimum length (8+ chars; 12+ recommended)
  No check against breached password lists
  Fix: validate against Have I Been Pwned API, enforce complexity

BRUTE FORCE / CREDENTIAL STUFFING:
  No rate limiting on login endpoint
  Attackers try millions of username/password pairs from leaked databases
  Fix: rate limit by IP + username, lockout after N failures, CAPTCHA

ACCOUNT ENUMERATION:
  Login returns 'User not found' vs 'Wrong password' — reveals valid usernames
  Password reset returns 'Email not registered' — reveals account existence
  Fix: return identical messages regardless of which check failed

INSECURE PASSWORD STORAGE:
  Storing passwords in plaintext or with MD5/SHA1 (reversible with rainbow tables)
  Fix: use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2id — never MD5/SHA1/SHA256 for passwords

MISSING SECURE FLAGS ON SESSION TOKENS:
  Session cookies without HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite
  Session IDs in URLs (?sessionId=abc) — logged by proxies, shared in URLs
  Fix: HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Lax cookies, never expose session in URL

NO MFA FOR HIGH-VALUE ACTIONS:
  No second factor for password changes, payment additions, privilege escalation
  Fix: require MFA for account changes and sensitive operations

questions.question: Your login endpoint returns 'User not found' for unregistered emails and 'Incorrect password' for registered ones. Why is this a security issue?
options: It's not an issue — giving more specific errors improves user experience
It allows account enumeration — attackers can confirm which email addresses have accounts, enabling targeted phishing and credential stuffing
It violates GDPR because it reveals database contents
questions.explanation: This is an account enumeration vulnerability. By returning different error messages, you're telling an attacker whether an email address is registered. They can automate this check: try 10,000 emails, note which get 'Incorrect password' (registered), and those become targets for credential stuffing (trying leaked passwords) or spear phishing. The fix: always return 'Invalid email or password' — the same message regardless of whether the email doesn't exist or the password is wrong. Same principle applies to password reset: return 'If that email is registered, you'll receive a link' rather than confirming/denying whether the email exists.

faq.q: Should I implement my own authentication or use a library?
faq.a: Use a battle-tested library or service (Passport.js, Auth.js/NextAuth, Clerk, Auth0, Supabase Auth) unless you have a compelling reason to build from scratch. Authentication has many subtle failure modes — timing attacks, session fixation, concurrent login handling, secure token generation — that libraries have already solved. If you do build it yourself, have a security expert review it. The cost of a breach far exceeds the time saved by rolling your own auth.

examples: The 2012 LinkedIn breach exposed 6.5 million password hashes — stored as unsalted SHA1. Crackers broke 90% of them within days using rainbow tables. Had LinkedIn used bcrypt, the same hardware would take centuries. LinkedIn later moved to bcrypt + salt, but the damage (credential stuffing attacks against users who reused those passwords) persisted for years

In 2016, 117 million LinkedIn credentials from the 2012 breach were sold on the dark web — 4 years later. Credential stuffing using those pairs was used to compromise accounts on GitHub, Yahoo, and other sites where users reused their LinkedIn password. This is why checking passwords against Have I Been Pwned at registration matters: if the password appeared in a breach, users will reuse it elsewhere, compounding the damage
